# Incident Report: MTA 2026-01-31 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Evidence Reviewed
Single artifact provided: `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (51,181 frames, 26.4 MB). No separate IDS/Suricata alert export was present in the evidence directory — all findings below are derived directly from packet analysis via `tshark`.

## Infected Host
| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.1.21.58** |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** (Intel NIC) |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** (NetBIOS/DHCP-confirmed; also broadcasts NetBIOS alias `WIN11OFFICE`) |
| Domain | WIN11OFFICE.COM (domain-joined, DC at 10.1.21.2) |
| Logged-in user | **gwyatt** (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS exchanges, `CNameString=gwyatt`, realm `WIN11OFFICE.COM`) |

## Malware Family and Attribution
**Attribution: behavioral, not signature-confirmed.** No AV/YARA verdict or IDS alert artifact was included in this evidence set, and the payload delivery itself occurred entirely inside TLS (no plaintext binary was recoverable, so no file hash could be computed for the dropped payload).

The observed activity is a **browser-based fingerprinting gate / traffic-distribution-system (TDS) chain leading to a commodity Windows info-stealer/loader**. Within a ~2-minute window (~t=45s to t=127s into the capture), the host was walked through six disposable, freshly-resolved lookalike domains, fronted by Cloudflare, before landing on a dedicated non-Cloudflare host (`whitepepper.su`) that:
1. Served JavaScript to the victim's own browser that fingerprints it (`navigator.platform`, `userAgent`, `hardwareConcurrency`, `deviceMemory`, WebGL renderer/vendor/extensions, etc.),
2. Received the fingerprint back via `act=log` POST callbacks tied to a persistent bot ID/token, and
3. Was then hit with **~20 separate short-lived TCP/TLS connections in rapid succession** (roughly 1 per second) — a classic C2 poll/heartbeat pattern, not normal web browsing.

This chain shape (fingerprint-and-gate → fake-update/CDN redirect chain with a large binary fetch → beaconing panel with bot id/token) is consistent with the fake-CAPTCHA/fake-browser-update ("ClickFix"-style) delivery method commonly used to drop commodity stealer/loader malware (e.g., Lumma-Stealer-style loaders). I cannot confirm the exact family name with certainty from this evidence alone — treat the family label as a behavioral hypothesis, not a confirmed identification.

## Indicators of Compromise

### C2 / gate endpoints (IP:port), in chronological order observed
| Time (rel.) | Domain | Resolved IP | Port | Role (evidence-based) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ~45.35s | hiyter.com | 104.21.22.231 (Cloudflare) | 443 | Redirect hop |
| ~45.92s | media.megafilehub4.lat | 104.21.48.156 (Cloudflare) | 443 | Redirect hop (~217 KB exchanged) |
| ~48.36s | arch.filemegahab4.sbs | 104.21.46.67 (Cloudflare) | 443 | **Large payload fetch — ~16 MB downloaded** over one TCP stream (10.1.21.58:54840↔104.21.46.67:443) |
| ~90.37s | whooptm.cyou | 62.72.32.156 | 443 | Redirect hop |
| ~122.8s | holiday-forever.cc | 80.97.160.24 | 443 | Redirect hop (~125 KB exchanged) |
| ~126.5s | communicationfirewall-security.cc | 104.21.9.36 (Cloudflare) | 443 | Redirect hop |
| ~92s–121.8s | **whitepepper.su** | **153.92.1.49** | **80 and 443** | **Fingerprinting gate / C2 panel.** Plaintext HTTP GET/POST on port 80; ~20 additional short repeated TLS connections on port 443 in a 1-per-second beacon pattern |

### Malicious domains
- whitepepper.su
- communicationfirewall-security.cc
- holiday-forever.cc
- whooptm.cyou
- arch.filemegahab4.sbs
- media.megafilehub4.lat
- hiyter.com

### Malicious URLs (observed in cleartext HTTP)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log` (POST — carries browser/hardware fingerprint exfil, confirmed by decoding `http.file_data`: navigator platform/userAgent/language/hardwareConcurrency/deviceMemory/WebGL vendor "Google Inc. (AMD)" / renderer "ANGLE (AMD, AMD Radeon R9 200 Series ...)")
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge` and matching `&act=log` POST variant
- `http://whitepepper.su/favicon.ico`

### Bot/session identifiers (persistent across requests — track as IOCs)
- `id = 3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C`
- `token = 842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b`

### Transferred files / hashes
**None recoverable.** All substantial data transfer (notably the ~16 MB object fetched from `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` / 104.21.46.67) occurred inside TLS with no key log present in the capture, so no file name or SHA256 could be extracted or computed. Objects that `tshark --export-objects http` initially surfaced (a PE32+ DLL, a Chrome-extension archive, a ZIP) could **not** be tied to any genuine HTTP request/response pair for this host when the HTTP transaction list was cross-checked directly (`http.request`/`http.response` fields show only the three legitimate/gate hosts above) — they are excluded from this report as unverified/likely tool artifacts rather than confirmed evidence.

## Summary
Host **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML (10.1.21.58, MAC 00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2)**, logged in as domain user **gwyatt**, was funneled through a six-domain Cloudflare-fronted redirect/fingerprinting chain culminating in check-ins to **whitepepper.su (153.92.1.49)**, exhibiting browser fingerprint exfiltration and stealer/loader-style beaconing behavior. No signature or file-hash confirmation of the specific malware family was possible from this capture alone; recommend isolating the host, capturing memory/disk for static malware identification, and blocking the seven domains/IPs listed above at the perimeter.
